planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall several weeks before the ground freezes, in well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Classic Rembrandt-type 'broken' tulip with ivory-white petals heavily flamed and feathered in rich cherry-red, the irregular streaking a heritage trait passed down from Dutch tulip-mania-era stock. Sturdy stems hold the large cupped blooms well above the foliage in mid-to-late spring, making it a favorite for recreating historic tulip borders. Because the color break is caused by a mild virus, keep it isolated from lily-flowered or other virus-susceptible tulips.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil before the ground freezes.

directions: A Rembrandt-group broken tulip with crisp white petals boldly streaked in deep purple-violet flames radiating up from the base. The jagged, feathered color break is a heritage trait propagated from offsets rather than reproduced true from seed. Long-lasting cupped flowers open in mid-spring on strong stems, giving excellent presence among other heirloom tulip plantings.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall; growers of this heirloom often pot bulbs to protect the delicate color break.

directions: One of the few surviving English Florists' Tulips, a 'Bizarre' broken type with golden-yellow petals densely flamed in black-maroon feathering that intensifies as the flower ages. Raised in the nineteenth century, it is still propagated by specialist florists' tulip societies and traditionally grown in pots under cover to keep the exhibition-quality petals pristine. It blooms later than most modern Dutch hybrids and increases slowly from offsets.
sources: Wakefield and North of England Tulip Society

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in a full-sun bed or border.

directions: A fringed tulip with glossy white petals edged in strawberry-red and trimmed with a fine crystalline fringe that catches the light. The bicolor red-and-white display becomes more pronounced as the flower ages and opens wider in sun. It blooms mid-to-late spring and pairs well with other fringed or parrot cultivars in cutting gardens.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in a sheltered, well-drained site to protect the ruffled petals.

directions: A parrot tulip with deeply cut, undulating petals in rose-pink edged and streaked with jade green, combining the ruffled parrot form with a viridiflora-style green flame. The twisted, wavy petal margins give each bloom an informal, almost orchid-like look. It flowers in late spring and benefits from a sheltered spot, since the fragile ruffled petals can be damaged by strong wind or heavy rain.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in sharply drained, sunny soil; this species naturalizes well left undisturbed.

directions: A dainty cultivar of the lady tulip with slender, pointed petals that are pale yellow flushed cherry-red along the outer edges, opening to reveal a soft yellow interior. Like the species, it holds its elegant wineglass form by day and closes at night, naturalizing readily in well-drained, sunny sites. Its wiry stems and narrow gray-green foliage give it a graceful, wildflower-like look in rock gardens and border edges.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil; ideal for rock gardens.

directions: A compact selection of the Central Asian species Tulipa batalinii with soft apricot-yellow petals flushing deeper apricot-orange toward the base. The small, slender buds open into neat star-shaped flowers above narrow, waxy blue-gray leaves. It is reliably perennial in sharply drained soil and is a staple of rock gardens and gravel plantings, where its diminutive scale and pastel coloring stand out in early-to-mid spring.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in very sharply drained soil; needs a hot, dry summer rest.

directions: A miniature species tulip from the mountains of Afghanistan and Central Asia, bearing clusters of small star-shaped flowers that are white with a yellow base, the petal backs tinged gray-green or purplish. Several blooms often open per bulb on short stems above grassy foliage, among the earliest tulips to flower in very early spring. It needs a hot, dry summer rest and sharp drainage to persist, making it best suited to rock gardens, troughs, or bulb frames.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun.

directions: A tiny species tulip native to Iran, closely related to Tulipa humilis, producing low clusters of pink to magenta-purple flowers with a small yellow eye at the base of each petal. Its narrow, slightly glaucous leaves lie close to the ground, and the flowers open flat in full sun on bright early-spring days. It thrives in gritty, sharply drained soil and is best grown in rock gardens or containers where its diminutive scale can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in very well-drained, sunny rock-garden soil.

directions: A species tulip native to the western Himalaya and parts of Afghanistan and Pakistan, with slender white petals flushed rose-purple on the reverse and a yellow basal blotch inside. The star-shaped flowers open wide on slim stems above narrow gray-green leaves in early-to-mid spring. It prefers a baking-hot, dry summer dormancy similar to other high-elevation Asian species tulips and performs best in very well-drained, sunny rock garden conditions.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in gritty, fast-draining soil that bakes dry in summer.

directions: A diminutive species tulip endemic to the mountains of Crete, bearing small star-shaped flowers in shades of pale pink to white with a yellow center, carried on wiry stems above narrow, grassy leaves. It flowers in early spring and, like many Mediterranean mountain species, requires a hot, dry summer rest to reliably return the following year. Its small scale makes it most at home in alpine troughs, raised beds, or gritty rock garden pockets.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in sharply drained, sunny rock-garden soil.

directions: A Central Asian species tulip from the mountains of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, with slender, pointed petals in bright yellow flushed red or bronze-pink on the outer surface. The elegant, somewhat nodding buds straighten and open wide in sunshine, revealing a glossy yellow interior. It is best grown in sharply drained, sunny rock garden conditions where its narrow, sometimes slightly wavy leaves and graceful form can be appreciated.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in a full-sun border.

directions: An heirloom single late (Darwin-type) tulip with large, long-oval blooms in soft lilac-mauve to heliotrope-blue, among the closest approaches to true blue found in historic tulip cultivars. Popular with heirloom bulb collectors for its unusual smoky-lavender coloring and sturdy, tall stems, it reliably perennializes in beds and borders. It combines nicely with white or apricot tulips for a soft, late-spring palette.
